tasks.question: Where is compression algorithm support implemented within the FITS image plugin system?
tasks.reference_answer: Compression algorithm support is not implemented within the FITS image plugin system in Pillow. The header parsing mechanism (src/PIL/FitsImagePlugin.py: line 27-40) reads standard FITS 80-character header blocks but does not process compression-related keywords such as GZIP, RICE, HCOMPRESS, PLIO, or other FITS compression standards. The image data is processed using a simple raw tile configuration (src/PIL/FitsImagePlugin.py: line 63) with no compression decoders. The deprecated FitsStubImagePlugin.py provides a handler registration mechanism (src/PIL/FitsStubImagePlugin.py: line 18-44) that could theoretically be extended to support custom compression handlers, but this approach has been explicitly deprecated since version 9.1.0 (src/PIL/FitsStubImagePlugin.py: line 27-32) with users directed to use the main FitsImagePlugin instead. The current implementation is limited to reading uncompressed FITS files only, as confirmed by the basic test coverage and documentation which makes no mention of compression capabilities.

tasks.question: Why do repeated calls to ImageFont operations cause progressive memory leaks that eventually lead to resource exhaustion in Pillow's FreeType integration?
tasks.reference_answer: Repeated calls to ImageFont operations cause progressive memory leaks because the FreeTypeFont class relies entirely on Python's garbage collection mechanism to release FreeType resources, which can be delayed or prevented by reference cycles or long-lived object references. The FreeTypeFont.__init__ method (src/PIL/ImageFont.py: line 177-219) creates a C extension FontObject via core.getfont() (src/_imagingft.c: line 118-209), which allocates a FT_Face structure and potentially font_bytes memory (src/_imagingft.c: line 172-183). The cleanup function font_dealloc (src/_imagingft.c: line 1214-1222) calls FT_Done_Face() and PyMem_Free() to release these resources, but it only executes when the Python FontObject is garbage collected. However, FreeTypeFont instances hold a reference to the FontObject in self.font (src/PIL/ImageFont.py: line 200-201, 215-216), and when font_bytes are loaded from memory, FreeTypeFont also holds self.font_bytes (src/PIL/ImageFont.py: line 199), creating potential reference cycles. More critically, if FreeTypeFont objects are stored in long-lived containers, passed between functions, or referenced by other objects, Python's garbage collector may not run frequently enough or may be unable to collect them due to reference cycles, causing FreeType resources to accumulate. The test_font_leaks.py file (Tests/test_font_leaks.py: line 6-23) demonstrates this issue, with memory leaks occurring after just a few iterations of draw.text() calls. Unlike Image objects which have explicit close() methods and context manager support (docs/releasenotes/6.1.0.rst: line 10-28), FreeTypeFont has no such mechanism, forcing reliance on non-deterministic garbage collection timing for resource cleanup.

tasks.question: Why does Pillow implement a dual-plugin architecture for FITS file format support using both FitsImagePlugin and FitsStubImagePlugin instead of a single unified plugin?
tasks.reference_answer: Pillow implements a dual-plugin architecture for FITS files as a transitional compatibility mechanism during the migration from external-handler-based support to native implementation. The FitsImagePlugin provides complete native FITS reading capability, parsing FITS headers, handling NAXIS and BITPIX values, and reading image data directly without external dependencies (src/PIL/FitsImagePlugin.py: line 21-64). The FitsStubImagePlugin serves as a legacy compatibility layer that allows applications with existing custom FITS handlers to continue functioning through the register_handler() function (src/PIL/FitsStubImagePlugin.py: line 18-43). When an external handler is registered, the stub plugin temporarily overrides the native plugin registration by removing and re-registering the format handler (src/PIL/FitsStubImagePlugin.py: line 36-43), using FitsImagePlugin._accept for file identification (src/PIL/FitsStubImagePlugin.py: line 42). Critically, the stub plugin internally delegates to FitsImagePlugin for metadata parsing (src/PIL/FitsStubImagePlugin.py: line 54-56), then applies the external handler for actual data loading via loader.open() (src/PIL/FitsStubImagePlugin.py: line 61-63). This architecture is unique among Pillow formats - other scientific formats like BUFR, GRIB, and HDF5 only provide stub plugins without native implementations (src/PIL/BufrStubImagePlugin.py, src/PIL/GribStubImagePlugin.py, src/PIL/Hdf5StubImagePlugin.py). The deprecation warning explicitly indicates this is a transitional design that will be removed in Pillow 10 (2023-07-01), with users encouraged to migrate to the native FitsImagePlugin (src/PIL/FitsStubImagePlugin.py: line 27-32, docs/deprecations.rst: line 136-143).

tasks.question: Why does PIL implement both full plugin implementations and stub plugin implementations for different image formats in its plugin architecture?
tasks.reference_answer: PIL implements both full and stub plugin architectures to serve distinct strategic purposes: full plugins provide optimal performance and zero dependencies for commonly used formats, while stub plugins enable support for specialized domain-specific formats without bloating PIL's codebase or adding complex dependencies. Full plugin implementations like BmpImagePlugin (src/PIL/BmpImagePlugin.py: line 62) provide complete native format support with comprehensive parsing, encoding, and decoding capabilities built directly into PIL. These plugins inherit from ImageFile.ImageFile (src/PIL/ImageFile.py: line 84) and contain extensive format-specific logic, such as BMP's complex header parsing for different compression schemes (src/PIL/BmpImagePlugin.py: line 70, 74-149), palette handling (src/PIL/BmpImagePlugin.py: line 218-247), and bit depth variations (src/PIL/BmpImagePlugin.py: line 40-48). This approach ensures optimal performance and eliminates external dependencies for commonly used image formats. In contrast, stub plugin implementations like BufrStubImagePlugin (src/PIL/BufrStubImagePlugin.py: line 35), GribStubImagePlugin (src/PIL/GribStubImagePlugin.py: line 35), and Hdf5StubImagePlugin (src/PIL/Hdf5StubImagePlugin.py: line 35) serve as adapter interfaces that delegate actual processing to external specialized handlers. These inherit from ImageFile.StubImageFile (src/PIL/ImageFile.py: line 315) and provide minimal format identification through _accept() methods (src/PIL/BufrStubImagePlugin.py: line 31-32, src/PIL/GribStubImagePlugin.py: line 31-32, src/PIL/Hdf5StubImagePlugin.py: line 31-32), but rely on external libraries registered via register_handler() functions (src/PIL/BufrStubImagePlugin.py: line 17-24, src/PIL/GribStubImagePlugin.py: line 17-24, src/PIL/Hdf5StubImagePlugin.py: line 17-24) to perform the actual image operations. The StubImageFile.load() method (src/PIL/ImageFile.py: line 326-335) delegates to the external handler by calling _load() to retrieve the registered handler, then transforms the stub object into the handler's image object. This stub pattern is specifically designed for specialized scientific and meteorological formats like BUFR (meteorological data), GRIB (weather data with complex embedded structures), and HDF5 (hierarchical scientific data), as documented in the image-file-formats handbook (docs/handbook/image-file-formats.rst: line 1405-1437). The stub approach allows PIL to maintain a consistent API surface for these domain-specific formats without incorporating complex, specialized parsing logic that would significantly increase PIL's codebase size and dependencies. The architecture also enables integration with dedicated scientific libraries that have deep expertise in these specialized format specifications, while keeping PIL's core focused on general-purpose image processing.

tasks.question: Why does Pillow's numpy array interface architecture use a dual conversion system with separate `__array__()` and `fromarray()` pathways instead of implementing a unified bidirectional array protocol?
tasks.reference_answer: Pillow implements separate conversion pathways because each direction faces distinct architectural constraints that cannot be efficiently unified. The PIL-to-numpy pathway through the __array__ method (src/PIL/Image.py: line 669-685) prioritizes memory efficiency and leverages PIL's internal data organization. It uses the _ArrayData wrapper class (src/PIL/Image.py: line 665-667) to expose PIL's internal byte data through numpy's __array_interface__ protocol, calling the _conv_type_shape function (src/PIL/Image.py: line 239-245) to determine appropriate shape and type string metadata based on PIL's mode system defined in ImageMode.py (src/PIL/ImageMode.py: line 43-90). The conversion relies on PIL's tobytes method to extract raw pixel data without unnecessary copying when possible, with special handling for binary mode '1' images that require bit-to-byte extension (src/PIL/Image.py: line 678-681). Conversely, the numpy-to-PIL pathway through fromarray (src/PIL/Image.py: line 2851-2921) prioritizes type safety and foreign array compatibility. It inspects incoming objects via their __array_interface__ (src/PIL/Image.py: line 2890) and maps array characteristics through the _fromarray_typemap lookup table (src/PIL/Image.py: line 2942-2966), which translates numpy dtype and shape combinations into PIL-compatible mode and rawmode pairs. When arrays are non-contiguous, it safely handles them by calling tobytes or tostring methods (src/PIL/Image.py: line 2915-2919) before passing data to frombuffer (src/PIL/Image.py: line 2794-2848). The frombuffer function can leverage zero-copy memory mapping for specific modes defined in _MAPMODES (src/PIL/Image.py: line 252, 2838-2846) when arrays are contiguous, using core.map_buffer() to share memory between PIL and numpy. The asymmetric design allows PIL to maintain strict control over its internal image data structures while accommodating numpy's array protocol expectations. Different memory management strategies are employed since PIL manages diverse internal formats and can leverage memory mapping for specific modes, while numpy expects contiguous typed arrays with predictable layouts.

tasks.question: How does PIL's plugin architecture ensure consistent API interfaces across different image format implementations when some plugins inherit format-specific attributes while others do not?
